title: Kentucky health officials confirm more measles cases in Commonwealth: What you need to know - NewsBreak
text: LEXINGTON, Ky. ( FOX 56 ) — Despite a majority of people having the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine, a July 8 news release from the Lexington-Fayette County Health Department announced the confirmation of 12 reported cases of measles in the Commonwealth this year. “If you look at the viruses that we have on Earth, actually, measles is one of the most contagious viruses that we have,” said Steve Davis, Lexington-Fayette County Health Department’s Medical Director. Nine of the confirmed cases were connected to an outbreak in Woodford and Fayette counties, most of them in unvaccinated individuals. Five of the nine were in Fayette County, all of whom were household contacts of the first Fayette County case. According to the Kentucky Cabinet for Health and Family Services, measles can lead to more serious infections like pneumonia, and in more severe cases, brain swelling and even death. “A big point to make is that measles also can be very serious. Very, very serious,” Davis said. What’s causing this? Davis said it is a nationwide issue where fewer children are getting properly immunized as they head into kindergarten. “Ballpark figures statewide right now, that number’s around 85%, where we used to be 93, 94, 95%,” he told FOX 56. If you are unvaccinated and you come into contact with someone with measles, Davis said there is a greater than 90% chance that you are going to come down with the viral infection. It brings a telltale red rash—plus an elevated temperature and what Davis called the “three C’s”: “Cough, conjunctivitis, which is a big old fancy word for your eye—the white of your eyes getting red—and coryza, which is a big old fancy word for runny nose,” said Davis. According to him, the best protection is to ensure that you are vaccinated. “If you’re properly immunized with the two doses of measles vaccine that children get, you have a 97% chance that you will not get the measles,” said Davis. “If you had one measles vaccination, you have about a 93% chance you won’t get the measles.” Of the infected individuals, health officials say there is no known additional risk to the public, but they are urging people to check their vaccination status. According to the health department, adults born after 1957 should have documentation of at least one dose of the MMR vaccine, and children should receive two doses: the first at 12-15 months old and the second at 4-6 years old.
